question.problem: Determine the interval on which the function $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}\,j-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k$ is differentiable.
question.worked_solution:
The vector-valued function $f(t)$ is defined on the interval $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).$ Let's study the differentiability of its components on this interval one by one.

- The derivative of  $\operatorname{sin}⁡3t$ is

$$
{(\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)}^{′}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $\operatorname{sin}⁡3t$ is differentiable on this interval.

- The derivative of  $\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}$ is

$$
{(\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1})}^{′}=\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}}.
$$

 
Since the derivative is not defined at $t=\pm 1,$ we conclude that  $\sqrt{{t}^{2}-1}$ is not differentiable at this points.

- The derivative of  $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is

$$
{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 
Since the derivative is defined for all the points on the interval $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ),$ we conclude that  $-\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ is differentiable on this interval.

Taking into account that all the components of $f(t)$ are differentiable for all the points on the interval $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ),$ except the points $t=\pm 1,$ we conclude that $f(t)$  is differentiable on $(-\infty ,-1)\cup (1,\infty ).$
